title: Past, present, future mind (section 18)
hook: past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped

segments.voice: Yesterday: suchness. The sutra says the name Tathagata means things just as they are. Your line: suchness. Did you look at one thing again, without its label? A new week starts. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

A story is told in the Zen tradition about a learned monk on the road, his pack full of his own commentaries on the Diamond Sutra. Hungry, he stops at a roadside stall to buy a snack from an old woman. She looks at the pack and asks what's in it. Notes on the Diamond Sutra, he says. Then she says, I have a question. If you can answer it, the snack is free. The sutra says past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped. So which mind is this snack for? He has no answer. Today, the line she quoted.
screen: `A MONK WITH HIS COMMENTARIES.` → `AN OLD WOMAN'S QUESTION.` → `WHICH MIND?`

segments.voice: First, the eyes. Section eighteen opens with a string of short questions. Does the Tathagata have the physical eye? He does, Subhuti says. The heavenly eye? The wisdom eye? The eye of the teaching? The eye of a Buddha? Yes, yes, yes, yes. Five ways of seeing, and the Buddha has every one. Second, the sand. The Buddha asks: picture as many rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and as many worlds as there are grains in all those rivers. Many? Very many, says Subhuti. And all the beings in all those worlds, the Buddha says, with all their kinds of minds, the Tathagata knows them. Third, the turn. Then why does he know them? Because, the sutra says, what are called minds are not minds; that is why they are called minds. The Buddha who sees every mind sees that none of them is a fixed, solid thing. Fourth, the three. Past mind can't be grasped. It's gone; what's left is memory, and memory is happening now. Future mind can't be grasped. It isn't here yet; what's here is planning, and planning is happening now. And present mind can't be grasped either. Reach for it, and by the time your hand closes, it has moved. That's what silenced the monk in the story. He had studied this line and written about it. But a snack is eaten now, and now can't be caught and held. Some readers hear despair in that. The sutra seems to hear freedom. A mind that can't be grasped also can't be trapped. Yesterday's mistake isn't a cell. Tomorrow's worry isn't a wall. Even this moment's mood is already on its way.
screen: `FIVE EYES, ALL OPEN.` · `EVERY MIND IN EVERY WORLD.` · `MINDS ARE NOT MINDS.` · `PAST, PRESENT, FUTURE: UNGRASPED.` · then, large: `CAN'T BE GRASPED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: try to grasp this moment. Settle, and breathe in. As the breath arrives, try to catch it, to hold this exact instant still. Notice what happens: the breath is already turning, already leaving. Try again on the next one. And the next. Don't strain. The point isn't to succeed. It's to feel, gently, that the moment keeps slipping through the fingers, and to see whether that feels like loss or like room. When a memory or a plan pulls you away, notice it, and let it go too. The bell holds the time.
Past. With present and future, one of the three minds the Diamond Sutra says can't be grasped. Today's word.
Your line: can't be grasped. Today, when an old regret or a future worry grips you, say the line once, and come back to whatever your hands are doing. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: The line about past, present and future mind is quoted in Chan and Zen teaching, and the story of the monk and the snack seller is told as a teaching tale about it.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: mind, heart-mind; section 18 says past, present and future mind can't be grasped.

trapdoor: what you thought: past, present and future are three places the mind can be.
what it means: none of the three can be grasped; minds are not minds, so they are called minds.
what a scholar hears: the five eyes and the sands of the Ganges set up the claim that the all-seeing Buddha sees no fixed mind.
